one_liner: Operator-overloading C++ AD library whose adjoint tape beats Adept 2 and CppAD by 1.1-2.3x on quant-finance gradients.
what_it_does: XAD computes derivatives of existing C++ code by replacing double with active types (e.g. Adouble / xad::AReal) and recording operations on a tape. It supports forward, adjoint (reverse) and higher-order modes, vector mode, checkpointing, an external-function interface and Eigen types. The API is not a drop-in for another AD library: you register inputs and outputs on a tape, seed the output adjoint and call computeAdjoints().
how_it_is_fast: Adjoint AD by operator overloading onto a tape (the benchmark repo labels XAD tape-based, like CppAD, while Adept 2 uses expression templates with stack recording); the internal tape layout is not documented in the pages read. An optional JIT backend interface supports record-once/replay-many for Monte Carlo; the commercial xad-codegen backend compiles the recorded graph to AVX2 native code and is 2-5x faster than the tape in the vendor's runs. Compile-time options trade speed for memory (XAD_REDUCED_MEMORY, XAD_TAPE_REUSE_SLOTS), force inlining (XAD_USE_STRONG_INLINE) or remove thread-local tape overhead (XAD_NO_THREADLOCAL).
when_to_use: Many-inputs/one-output gradients (risk sensitivities, calibration Jacobians) where finite differences cost O(N) primal runs; the vendor run shows about 70x over FD at 161 inputs
Monte Carlo pricing and XVA-style workloads in existing double-based C++ code, including QuantLib (via QuantLibAAD)
Projects that need higher-order derivatives, checkpointing for tape memory, or hooks for external (non-AD) functions
Codebases already using Eigen that need AD through Eigen expressions
AGPL-compatible projects, or teams willing to buy the commercial licence
when_not_to_use: Proprietary/closed-source distribution without a commercial licence: the library is AGPL-3.0
If you expect the headline benchmark speeds for free: the fastest column is xad-codegen, a closed commercial add-on
Small statically-known expression graphs where an expression-template-only library such as FastAD may be faster (not measured head-to-head here)
Very long recordings on memory-tight machines: reverse-mode tapes grow with operation count unless you use checkpointing
Tensor/ML-style workloads; XAD targets scalar operator-overloading AD, not batched tensor kernels

integration.dependencies: none (Eigen optional; xad-codegen optional and commercial)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; GCC 7+, Clang 11+, Apple Clang 11+, Visual Studio 2019+; CMake 3.15.2+
integration.platforms: Linux, macOS, Windows; x86-64 with SSE2/AVX/AVX2/AVX512 selectable via XAD_SIMD_OPTION (default AVX), Apple M1 option on macOS
integration.thread_safety: Tapes are thread-local by default (one active tape per thread); XAD_NO_THREADLOCAL disables this for single-threaded use

gotchas: Tape behaviour is fixed at build time through CMake options written into a generated Config.hpp; build your project and XAD with the same compiler and flags (the install guide warns about this)
XAD_ALLOW_INT_CONVERSION is ON by default: real-to-int conversions compile silently and can drop dependencies from the derivative
Moving from tape to xad-codegen requires rewriting data-dependent branches as xad::less(a,b).If(then,else) so the recorded graph is branch-free
The benchmark harness pulls XAD, CppAD, Adept and autodiff from their main/master branches, so the numbers are not tied to fixed versions
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick XAD over FastAD when you need a maintained, general-purpose AD with forward/reverse/higher-order modes, checkpointing, Eigen support and QuantLib integration; FastAD's own paper reports bigger margins over Adept on small expression benchmarks but is narrower in scope. The other siblings (DGEMM kernels, tinyBLAS, MNN, T-MAC, TCL, nanoinfer) are ML/linear-algebra kernels, not AD libraries.
verified_claims_summary: In the vendor's ad-benchmarks repo (GCC 13.3, -O3 -mavx2 -mfma, Intel Xeon Platinum 8488C, Ubuntu 24.04, median of 10 iterations after warmup), open-source XAD tape-mode gradients took 40 ms (Heston MC), 8.4 ms (SABR), 2.6 s (XVA CVA) and 1.00 s (LIBOR swaption), against Adept 2 at 91 ms / 19 ms / 7.1 s / 1.15 s and CppAD at 268 ms / 32 ms / 8.0 s / 4.57 s. The commercial xad-codegen column (21 ms / 4.9 ms / 0.57 s / 0.31 s) cannot be reproduced from public code.
status_note: Actively maintained (last commit September 2026) with a commercial backer (Xcelerit); usable as source under AGPL-3.0, with a paid licence for closed-source use and for xad-codegen.
